stimuli.title: Six friends at a round table, with favourite games
stimuli.content:
Six friends Anupama, Bhushan, Gulzar, Madhavi, Rajat and Tanvir sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Each likes a different game among Carrom, Checkers, Chess, Ludo, Pachisi and Scrabble. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise.)

- Rajat sits second to the right of Anupama.
- Madhavi sits immediately to the left of Rajat.
- The person who likes Chess sits opposite Anupama, and that person is Gulzar.
- Tanvir is not an immediate neighbour of Gulzar.
- The person who likes Carrom sits immediately to the right of Gulzar.
- Anupama likes Ludo and Rajat likes Scrabble.
- Madhavi does not like Pachisi.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Put Anupama at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Rajat = 2, Madhavi = 1 (immediately to Rajat's left), Gulzar (Chess) = 3, opposite Anupama.
Step 2: Seats 4 and 5 remain for Bhushan and Tanvir. Seat 4 is next to Gulzar, so Tanvir = 5 and Bhushan = 4.
Step 3: Carrom is immediately to Gulzar's right: seat 4, Bhushan. Anupama Ludo, Rajat Scrabble; Checkers and Pachisi remain for Madhavi and Tanvir, and Madhavi does not like Pachisi, so Madhavi Checkers and Tanvir Pachisi.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person | Game |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anupama | Ludo |
| 1 | Madhavi | Checkers |
| 2 | Rajat | Scrabble |
| 3 | Gulzar | Chess |
| 4 | Bhushan | Carrom |
| 5 | Tanvir | Pachisi |

stimuli.title: Four men and four women seated alternately
stimuli.content:
Eight persons sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Four of them — Jaiwant, Mahesh, Prabal and Sudhir — are men, and the other four — Kalpita, Rupali, Swati and Vaishali — are women. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise.)

- Men and women sit alternately.
- Sudhir sits opposite Jaiwant.
- Swati sits immediately to the right of Sudhir.
- Rupali sits second to the left of Swati.
- Prabal sits immediately to the left of Rupali.
- Vaishali is an immediate neighbour of both Mahesh and Jaiwant.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Put Jaiwant at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Men take the even seats and women the odd seats.
Step 2: Sudhir = 4 (opposite Jaiwant); Swati = 5 (to his right); Rupali = 3 (second to Swati's left); Prabal = 2 (immediately to Rupali's left). Mahesh takes the last man's seat, 6.
Step 3: Vaishali neighbours both Mahesh (6) and Jaiwant (0): seat 7. Kalpita = 1.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Jaiwant |
| 1 | Kalpita |
| 2 | Prabal |
| 3 | Rupali |
| 4 | Sudhir |
| 5 | Swati |
| 6 | Mahesh |
| 7 | Vaishali |

stimuli.title: A rectangular table with outward-facing end seats
stimuli.content:
Six persons Hiranya, Jasmeet, Keshava, Lopamudra, Nakul and Revati sit around a rectangular table. The longer sides of the table are to the north and south, and each has two seats; the shorter sides are to the west and east, and each has one seat. The four persons on the longer sides face the centre of the table, while the two persons at the shorter (end) sides face away from the table. Seats on the north side are directly across from the seats on the south side, and the west-end seat is directly across from the east-end seat. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise; facing outside, it is the next seat clockwise.)

- Nakul sits at the west end of the table.
- Revati sits immediately to the right of Nakul.
- Keshava sits directly across the table from Revati.
- Jasmeet sits second to the right of Keshava.
- Lopamudra sits immediately to the left of Jasmeet.
stimuli.solution:
Going anticlockwise from the west end the seats are: west end, south-west, south-east, east end, north-east, north-west.
Step 1: Nakul (west end) faces outside, so his right is clockwise: Revati = north-west.
Step 2: Keshava is across from Revati: south-west. He faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: south-east, then the east end — Jasmeet.
Step 3: Jasmeet faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Lopamudra = north-east. Hiranya takes the last seat, south-east.

| Seat | Person | Facing |
|---|---|---|
| west end | Nakul | outside |
| south side, west seat | Keshava | centre |
| south side, east seat | Hiranya | centre |
| east end | Jasmeet | outside |
| north side, east seat | Lopamudra | centre |
| north side, west seat | Revati | centre |

stimuli.title: Twelve chairs around a square table, two vacant
stimuli.content:
A square table has three chairs along each side — one at each end of the side and one in the middle — so there are twelve chairs, equally spaced around the table. Going round the table, the last chair of one side is next to the first chair of the next side. Ten persons Anvita, Bhargav, Chaitra, Haridas, Indumati, Kumud, Laxman, Mandakini, Nachiket and Parimal sit on ten of the chairs, all facing the centre, and two chairs are vacant. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next chair anticlockwise. Vacant chairs are counted as chairs.)

- Anvita sits in the middle chair of a side, and Kumud sits directly opposite her (in the middle chair of the opposite side).
- Laxman sits third to the right of Kumud.
- Chaitra sits second to the right of Anvita, and Nachiket sits immediately to the right of Anvita.
- The two vacant chairs are on the same side of the table; it is neither Anvita's side nor Kumud's side.
- Bhargav sits immediately to the left of a vacant chair.
- Haridas sits on the same side as Kumud, but not in the middle chair, and Mandakini sits immediately to the left of Haridas.
- Indumati sits in the middle chair of a side.
stimuli.solution:
Number the chairs 0 to 11 anticlockwise so that Anvita is in chair 1, the middle of side A (chairs 0–2); side B has chairs 3–5, side C 6–8 and side D 9–11.
Step 1: Kumud = 7 (middle of side C). Laxman = 7 + 3 = 10. Nachiket = 2, Chaitra = 3.
Step 2: The vacant chairs share a side other than A and C. On side B, chair 3 is Chaitra's, so the vacant chairs would be 4 and 5; then Bhargav would have to be in chair 3 or 4 — impossible. So the vacant chairs are on side D: 9 and 11 (Laxman has 10), and Bhargav = 8 (immediately to the left of chair 9).
Step 3: Haridas is on side C but not in the middle; chair 8 is Bhargav's, so Haridas = 6 and Mandakini = 5. Indumati takes the middle chair 4, and Parimal the last chair, 0.

| Side | Chairs (anticlockwise) |
|---|---|
| A | Parimal, Anvita, Nachiket |
| B | Chaitra, Indumati, Mandakini |
| C | Haridas, Kumud, Bhargav |
| D | vacant, Laxman, vacant |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six curtain colours
stimuli.content:
Six persons Bhanu, Chandana, Girish, Purab, Ujjwal and Vasanti live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each has curtains of a different colour among Beige, Maroon, Mauve, Teal, Turquoise and Violet.

- Purab lives on floor 4, and Chandana lives immediately below Purab.
- Vasanti lives on the topmost floor.
- Only one person lives between Bhanu and Chandana.
- Girish lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- Ujjwal lives on a floor below Bhanu's floor.
- Bhanu has Teal curtains, and the person with Maroon curtains lives immediately above him.
- Girish has Beige curtains, and the person with Mauve curtains lives immediately above Girish.
- Chandana has neither Violet nor Mauve curtains.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Purab = 4, Chandana = 3, Vasanti = 6. Bhanu is two floors from Chandana: floor 1 or 5.
Step 2: Ujjwal lives below Bhanu, so Bhanu cannot be on floor 1: Bhanu = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain for Girish and Ujjwal; Girish is on an odd floor, so Girish = 1 and Ujjwal = 2.
Step 3: Bhanu Teal ⇒ Maroon on floor 6 (Vasanti). Girish Beige ⇒ Mauve on floor 2 (Ujjwal). Turquoise and Violet remain for Chandana and Purab; Chandana is not Violet, so Chandana Turquoise and Purab Violet.

| Floor | Person | Curtains |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Vasanti | Maroon |
| 5 | Bhanu | Teal |
| 4 | Purab | Violet |
| 3 | Chandana | Turquoise |
| 2 | Ujjwal | Mauve |
| 1 | Girish | Beige |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and their potted plants
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abhijit, Deepali, Faiyaz, Kamakshi, Leeladhar, Ojaswini and Rishi live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each keeps a different number of potted plants among 4, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15 and 18.

- The person who keeps 18 plants lives on floor 5, and Kamakshi lives two floors below that person.
- Kamakshi keeps exactly half as many plants as the person who lives immediately above her.
- The person who keeps 15 plants lives immediately below Kamakshi.
- Rishi lives on the topmost floor and keeps fewer plants than Kamakshi.
- Only two persons live between Rishi and Faiyaz.
- Abhijit lives on a floor above Faiyaz's floor and keeps the second-smallest number of plants.
- Deepali keeps an odd number of plants, and Leeladhar keeps fewer plants than Deepali.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: 18 plants on floor 5; Kamakshi = 3; 15 plants on floor 2.
Step 2: Kamakshi's count doubled must be on floor 4. Possible pairs from the list: 6 and 12, or 9 and 18 — but 18 is on floor 5, so Kamakshi keeps 6 and floor 4 has 12.
Step 3: Rishi = 7 with fewer than 6 plants: 4. Faiyaz is three floors below Rishi: floor 4 (12 plants).
Step 4: Abhijit is above Faiyaz with 7 plants; floor 5 has 18, so Abhijit = 6. Floor 1 then has 9 plants.
Step 5: Deepali, Leeladhar and Ojaswini take floors 1 (9), 2 (15) and 5 (18). Deepali's count is odd (9 or 15) and Leeladhar has fewer than Deepali: if Deepali had 9, nobody left would have fewer, so Deepali = floor 2 (15), Leeladhar = floor 1 (9) and Ojaswini = floor 5 (18).

| Floor | Person | Plants |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Rishi | 4 |
| 6 | Abhijit | 7 |
| 5 | Ojaswini | 18 |
| 4 | Faiyaz | 12 |
| 3 | Kamakshi | 6 |
| 2 | Deepali | 15 |
| 1 | Leeladhar | 9 |

stimuli.title: Seven floors, three professions, no two alike adjacent
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Gobind, Harleen, Jayanti, Madhur, Nirupama, Oorja and Shailesh live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each of them is a Doctor, a Lawyer or a Teacher.

- Three of them are Doctors, two are Lawyers and two are Teachers.
- No two persons of the same profession live on adjacent floors.
- Madhur is a Teacher and lives on floor 4.
- Oorja is a Doctor and lives on the topmost floor.
- Harleen lives immediately below Madhur and is not a Doctor.
- Gobind lives on floor 1 and has the same profession as Oorja.
- Jayanti is a Lawyer.
- Shailesh lives on a floor below Nirupama's floor.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Madhur (Teacher) = 4, Oorja (Doctor) = 7, Gobind (Doctor) = 1, Harleen = 3. Harleen is not a Doctor, and as Madhur's neighbour cannot be a Teacher: Harleen is a Lawyer.
Step 2: Floor 2 lies between a Doctor (1) and a Lawyer (3), so it is a Teacher. The professions left are one Doctor and one Lawyer for floors 5 and 6; floor 6 is next to Oorja (Doctor), so floor 6 is the Lawyer and floor 5 the Doctor.
Step 3: Jayanti is a Lawyer, so she is on floor 6. Shailesh is below Nirupama, so Shailesh = 2 (Teacher) and Nirupama = 5 (Doctor).

| Floor | Person | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Oorja | Doctor |
| 6 | Jayanti | Lawyer |
| 5 | Nirupama | Doctor |
| 4 | Madhur | Teacher |
| 3 | Harleen | Lawyer |
| 2 | Shailesh | Teacher |
| 1 | Gobind | Doctor |

stimuli.title: Four floors with three flats each, three vacant
stimuli.content:
A four-storey building (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 4 the topmost) has three flats on each floor: West, Middle and East. Each flat is directly above the flat of the same name on the floor below. Nine persons Ajeet, Bansi, Champa, Dilip, Fulmani, Gokul, Hemangini, Indraneel and Jagjit live in nine of the twelve flats, one person per flat, and the other three flats are vacant.

- Exactly three flats are vacant, and no two vacant flats are on the same floor.
- Gokul lives in the Middle flat of floor 3, and the flat directly below his flat is vacant.
- Ajeet lives directly above Gokul, and the East flat of Ajeet's floor is vacant.
- Bansi lives in a West flat on an even-numbered floor, and Dilip lives on the same floor as Bansi.
- Hemangini lives directly below Bansi, and Fulmani lives directly above Bansi.
- Champa lives directly above Dilip.
- Jagjit lives on the same floor as Hemangini, in the East flat.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gokul = 3-Middle, 2-Middle vacant; Ajeet = 4-Middle, 4-East vacant. Floors 2 and 4 now have their vacant flat, so the third vacant flat is on floor 1 or 3.
Step 2: Bansi is in a West flat on floor 2 or 4. If Bansi were in 4-West, Fulmani would have to be above floor 4 — impossible. So Bansi = 2-West, Hemangini = 1-West, Fulmani = 3-West. Dilip is on floor 2: 2-East (2-Middle is vacant). Champa = 3-East, above Dilip.
Step 3: Jagjit = 1-East. Floor 3 is now full, so the third vacant flat is on floor 1: 1-Middle. Indraneel takes the last flat, 4-West.

| Floor | West | Middle | East |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | Indraneel | Ajeet | vacant |
| 3 | Fulmani | Gokul | Champa |
| 2 | Bansi | vacant | Dilip |
| 1 | Hemangini | vacant | Jagjit |

stimuli.title: Ten floors, seven residents, three vacant floors
stimuli.content:
A building has ten floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 10 (topmost). Seven persons Ketki, Murari, Navneet, Padmini, Rehaan, Sevanti and Trilok live in it, one person per floor, so exactly three floors are vacant.

- The lowermost and topmost floors are both occupied.
- Trilok lives on floor 7, and Murari lives immediately below Trilok.
- Ketki lives below Trilok; of the floors between Ketki and Trilok, exactly two are vacant and exactly one is occupied.
- Sevanti lives on an odd-numbered floor below Ketki's floor.
- Padmini lives immediately above Trilok.
- Only one person lives above Navneet.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Trilok = 7, Murari = 6, Padmini = 8.
Step 2: Between Ketki and Trilok there are exactly three floors (two vacant, one occupied), so Ketki = 3. Murari (6) is the occupied one, so floors 4 and 5 are vacant.
Step 3: Sevanti is on an odd floor below 3: floor 1. That leaves one more vacant floor among 2, 9 and 10, with Navneet and Rehaan to place; floor 10 is occupied.
Step 4: Only one person lives above Navneet. If Navneet were on floor 2, many would be above him; so Navneet = 9, Rehaan = 10, and floor 2 is vacant.

| Floor | Resident |
|---|---|
| 10 | Rehaan |
| 9 | Navneet |
| 8 | Padmini |
| 7 | Trilok |
| 6 | Murari |
| 5 | vacant |
| 4 | vacant |
| 3 | Ketki |
| 2 | vacant |
| 1 | Sevanti |

stimuli.title: Six saplings planted from June to November
stimuli.content:
Six persons Anokhi, Girdhar, Kanishka, Maitreyi, Pankaj and Suhani each plant one sapling in the same year, one person in each month from June to November. Each plants a different tree among Ashoka, Banyan, Jamun, Mango, Neem and Peepal.

- Kanishka plants in the last of the six months, and she plants the Ashoka.
- Girdhar plants in a month that has 30 days.
- Pankaj plants before Girdhar, and only two persons plant between them.
- The Neem sapling is planted in June.
- Anokhi plants in the month immediately after Pankaj's month, and she plants the Mango.
- Maitreyi plants in a month after Suhani's month.
- The Banyan is planted in the month immediately before the Ashoka.
- Suhani does not plant the Peepal.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kanishka = November (Ashoka). Girdhar's month has 30 days: June, September or November; Pankaj is three months before him, so Girdhar = September and Pankaj = June (Neem).
Step 2: Anokhi = July (Mango). August and October remain for Suhani and Maitreyi; Maitreyi is later, so Suhani = August and Maitreyi = October.
Step 3: Banyan is immediately before Ashoka (November): October, Maitreyi. Jamun and Peepal remain for Suhani and Girdhar; Suhani is not Peepal, so Suhani Jamun and Girdhar Peepal.

| Month | Person | Tree |
|---|---|---|
| June | Pankaj | Neem |
| July | Anokhi | Mango |
| August | Suhani | Jamun |
| September | Girdhar | Peepal |
| October | Maitreyi | Banyan |
| November | Kanishka | Ashoka |

stimuli.title: Six birth years, six birth months, ages on 1 June 2026
stimuli.content:
Six persons Avantika, Dinkar, Gurpreet, Mallika, Naresh and Shobhit were born in six different years among 1981, 1986, 1992, 1995, 1999 and 2004, and in six different months among January, March, May, July, September and November (one year and one month each). Ages are counted in completed years as on 1 June 2026: a person whose birthday month is later in the year than June has not yet had a 2026 birthday on that date.

- The person born in 1992 was born in March.
- Gurpreet is the youngest of the six and was born in January.
- Dinkar is the oldest of the six.
- As on 1 June 2026, Mallika is 30 years old and Avantika is 34 years old (in completed years).
- Naresh was born in May, and he is younger than Mallika.
- Shobhit was born in July, in a year before Avantika's year.
- Mallika was born in the latest of the six months.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gurpreet = January 2004 (youngest); Dinkar = 1981 (oldest).
Step 2: Avantika is 34 on 1 June 2026: born in 1992 with a birthday by June, or in 1991 with a later birthday — 1991 is not in the list, so Avantika = 1992, and the 1992-born person was born in March: Avantika = March 1992.
Step 3: Mallika is 30: 1996 with an early birthday (not in the list) or 1995 with a birthday after June. So Mallika = 1995, and she has the latest month, November.
Step 4: Shobhit = July, in a year before 1992: 1986 (1981 is Dinkar's). Naresh = May, younger than Mallika: 1999. Dinkar takes the last month, September.

| Person | Year | Month | Age on 1 June 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dinkar | 1981 | September | 44 |
| Shobhit | 1986 | July | 39 |
| Avantika | 1992 | March | 34 |
| Mallika | 1995 | November | 30 |
| Naresh | 1999 | May | 27 |
| Gurpreet | 2004 | January | 22 |

stimuli.title: Six visits on the weekends of August 2026
stimuli.content:
A heritage museum is open to visitors only on Saturdays and Sundays. Six persons Aparna, Gajendra, Kaushiki, Manohar, Riddhima and Tejpal each visit it once in August 2026, on six different dates. 1 August 2026 is a Saturday.

- Kaushiki visits on the third Saturday of the month, and Gajendra visits on the day after Kaushiki.
- Riddhima visits on the last Saturday of the month.
- Tejpal visits exactly one week after Gajendra.
- Aparna visits exactly two weeks before Kaushiki.
- Manohar visits on a Sunday before Kaushiki, but not on the same weekend as Aparna.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: The Saturdays are 1, 8, 15, 22 and 29 August and the Sundays 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 August.
Step 2: Kaushiki = 15 (third Saturday), Gajendra = 16, Tejpal = 23, Riddhima = 29 (last Saturday), Aparna = 15 − 14 = 1.
Step 3: Manohar visits on a Sunday before the 15th: the 2nd or the 9th. The 2nd is on Aparna's weekend (1–2 August), so Manohar = 9.

| Date | Day | Visitor |
|---|---|---|
| 1 August | Saturday | Aparna |
| 9 August | Sunday | Manohar |
| 15 August | Saturday | Kaushiki |
| 16 August | Sunday | Gajendra |
| 23 August | Sunday | Tejpal |
| 29 August | Saturday | Riddhima |

stimuli.title: Eight meetings in morning and afternoon slots
stimuli.content:
A branch manager holds two meetings a day — one in the morning and one in the afternoon — from Monday to Thursday of a week, so there are eight meeting slots. Eight customers Aalok, Bhupesh, Daya, Hemraj, Kanika, Mohsin, Rewa and Tarini each have one meeting, in different slots. (Monday morning is the first slot and Thursday afternoon the last; slots are counted in this order.)

- Hemraj's meeting is on Wednesday afternoon.
- Aalok meets before Hemraj, and only one meeting is held between their meetings.
- Kanika meets on the same day as Aalok.
- Mohsin's meeting is the last of the week, and Bhupesh meets on the same day as Mohsin.
- Tarini meets in a morning slot on a day after Kanika's day.
- Rewa meets in an afternoon slot.
stimuli.solution:
Number the slots 1 (Monday morning) to 8 (Thursday afternoon).
Step 1: Hemraj = 6 (Wednesday afternoon). Aalok = 4 (Tuesday afternoon), so Kanika = 3 (Tuesday morning).
Step 2: Mohsin = 8 and Bhupesh = 7 (Thursday morning).
Step 3: Tarini has a morning slot on a day after Tuesday: Wednesday morning (5), as Thursday morning is taken.
Step 4: Slots 1 and 2 remain; Rewa takes the afternoon slot (2) and Daya slot 1.

| Day | Morning | Afternoon |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Daya | Rewa |
| Tuesday | Kanika | Aalok |
| Wednesday | Tarini | Hemraj |
| Thursday | Bhupesh | Mohsin |

stimuli.title: Six insurance employees: posts and joining years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Ashwath, Deeksha, Faraaz, Ishika, Tushita and Yashwant of an insurance company hold six different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Zonal Head, Regional Head, Branch Head, Sales Manager, Agent Supervisor and Agent Trainee. Each joined the company in a different year among 2009, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2023. Seniority of post does not depend on the year of joining.

- Ishika is senior to all the others, and the person who joined in 2009 is immediately junior to her.
- Faraaz joined the earliest of all.
- Deeksha is the most junior, and she joined six years after Ashwath.
- Ashwath is immediately senior to Tushita, who joined in the latest year.
- Yashwant joined in 2017, five years after Ishika, and he is senior to Ashwath.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Ishika = Zonal Head. Faraaz joined in 2009, so he is immediately junior to her: Regional Head. Deeksha = Agent Trainee.
Step 2: Tushita joined in 2023, Yashwant in 2017 and Ishika in 2012. The years left are 2014 and 2020 for Ashwath and Deeksha, six years apart: Ashwath 2014, Deeksha 2020.
Step 3: Branch Head, Sales Manager and Agent Supervisor remain for Ashwath, Tushita and Yashwant, with Ashwath immediately above Tushita and Yashwant above Ashwath: Yashwant Branch Head, Ashwath Sales Manager, Tushita Agent Supervisor.

| Post | Employee | Joined |
|---|---|---|
| Zonal Head | Ishika | 2012 |
| Regional Head | Faraaz | 2009 |
| Branch Head | Yashwant | 2017 |
| Sales Manager | Ashwath | 2014 |
| Agent Supervisor | Tushita | 2023 |
| Agent Trainee | Deeksha | 2020 |

stimuli.title: Five two-letter code words for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the words zu, mi, ro, te and fa are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A zu B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B'; 'A mi B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B'; 'A ro B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B'; 'A te B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A fa B' means 'A is not greater than B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: zu means >, mi means <, ro means =, te means ≥ and fa means ≤ ('not smaller than' allows greater or equal; 'not greater than' allows smaller or equal). Rewrite each statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain, and test each conclusion along the chain.

stimuli.title: Two-letter code words for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode each expression pair by pair from left to right, draw the small family tree it describes, and then read the asked relation off the tree. Genders come from the words used: mother, daughter and sister are female; brother and husband are male.

stimuli.title: Three coded sentences about a city
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'clean the city' is written as 'ka mo ri',
'the city sleeps' is written as 'mo ri ze', and
'city lights glow' is written as 'ri pu lo'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: 'city' is the only word in all three sentences, and 'ri' the only code in all three: city = ri. Sentences 1 and 2 share 'the city' and the codes 'mo ri', so the = mo. The leftovers give clean = ka and sleeps = ze. In sentence 3, 'lights' and 'glow' share the codes 'pu' and 'lo', and nothing tells which is which.

stimuli.title: A two-step code: position shifts, then reversal for vowel-initial words
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language, every word is coded in two steps.
Step 1: Each letter in an odd position of the word (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) is replaced by the letter two places after it in the English alphabet, and each letter in an even position (2nd, 4th, …) by the letter one place before it. The alphabet wraps round (Y → A, Z → B, A → Z).
Step 2: If the word begins with a vowel, the letters obtained in step 1 are written in reverse order; otherwise they are kept in the same order.
stimuli.solution: Work letter by letter: +2 for the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … letters and −1 for the 2nd, 4th, … letters, wrapping round the alphabet. Then reverse the result only if the original word starts with A, E, I, O or U. To decode, undo step 2 first (reverse if the word might start with a vowel) and then shift back.

stimuli.title: Warning before the strike
stimuli.content:
Lightning kills more people in India each year than most other natural hazards, yet it rarely makes headlines. Unlike a cyclone or a flood, which can be tracked for days, a lightning strike is over in a fraction of a second, and its victims are usually scattered: a farmer in a field, a herder on a hillside, a group sheltering under a tree.

Most of these deaths happen in rural areas during the pre-monsoon and monsoon months, when thunderstorms build up quickly in the afternoon. People working outdoors are the most exposed. Many of them believe that a tall tree offers safety from the rain, but a lone tree is in fact one of the most dangerous places to stand, because lightning tends to strike the highest point in an open area.

In recent years, weather scientists have set up networks of sensors that detect the electrical activity of a storm as it forms. This allows them to issue warnings for a particular district from about thirty minutes to a few hours in advance. Several states now send these alerts as text messages, and free mobile apps show whether a storm is approaching the user's location.

A warning, however, is useful only if people know what to do with it. Officials therefore combine the alerts with simple advice. People caught outdoors should move into a solid building or a closed vehicle. If no shelter is near, they should keep away from trees, poles and water, and crouch low with their feet together rather than lie flat on the ground. They should also wait for about half an hour after the last thunder before going out again.

Experts say that awareness campaigns in schools and village meetings have already helped to reduce deaths in some districts. Their aim is modest but important: to turn a few minutes of warning into a few minutes of safe action.

stimuli.title: Money you can feel
stimuli.content:
For most people, telling one currency note from another takes only a glance. For the millions of Indians who are blind or have poor eyesight, it can be a daily struggle, and a mistake can be costly: a shopkeeper might hand back a ten-rupee note in place of a hundred, and the customer would never know.

Banknote designers try to help in several ways. Notes of different values are made in different sizes, so that a person can compare their length and width with the fingers. Many notes also carry marks printed in raised ink, such as small lines or shapes near the edge, which can be felt by touch. The large numerals and strong colours used on new notes are meant to help people whose sight is weak but not entirely lost.

These features do not always work as intended. When a new series of notes is introduced, older notes of the same value may stay in use for years, so people have to learn two sets of sizes. Raised printing tends to wear away as a note passes from hand to hand, and a note that has been folded, crumpled or soaked may be hard to read by touch at all. Some notes of neighbouring values are also so close in size that the difference is difficult to feel.

Technology now offers another aid. Mobile phone apps can identify a note when it is held in front of the camera and announce its value aloud, and some work even without an internet connection. Users say the apps are helpful, but they also point out that pulling out a phone for every transaction is slow, and not everyone owns a smartphone.

Organisations that work with the visually impaired argue that the best solution is a mix: notes designed with touch in mind from the very start, coins that are easy to tell apart, and apps for those who want them. Money, they say, should be usable by everyone who earns it.

stimuli.title: A number with a past
stimuli.content:
When a person stops using a mobile number, it does not disappear. After a period of inactivity, telecom operators may deactivate the connection and, some months later, issue the same number to a new customer. Numbers are a limited resource, and recycling them is a normal practice around the world. In an age of digital banking, however, it has created an unexpected risk.

Most bank accounts today are linked to a mobile number. The bank sends one-time passwords, transaction alerts and balance messages to that number, and many apps use it to identify the customer. If the old owner of a number forgets to update the bank, those messages may now reach a stranger. In the worst cases, a person who receives someone else's one-time passwords and has a few other details can reset passwords or approve payments.

The problem usually arises from neglect rather than crime. People change numbers when they move to a new city, switch operators or let a second SIM card lapse, and updating every bank, insurer and government service is tedious. Elderly customers and those who rarely use their accounts are especially likely to overlook it.

Banks and regulators have responded in several ways. Some banks now check whether a registered number has recently changed hands and ask the customer to confirm it before sending sensitive messages. Customers are urged to update their contact details whenever they give up a number, and to read alerts carefully, since an unfamiliar message may be the first sign that their details are out of date.

The episode is a reminder that security depends not only on strong technology but also on the ordinary links between a person and their accounts. A mobile number feels permanent to the person who uses it. To the network, it is merely on loan.

stimuli.title: Counting what hides
stimuli.content:
Counting tigers sounds simple until one tries it. The animals are shy, mostly active at night and spread across thick forest, so a direct head-count is impossible. For decades, Indian forest departments relied instead on pugmarks, the footprints that tigers leave on soft ground. Staff would trace the prints and try to tell individuals apart by their shape and size.

The method had obvious weaknesses. Prints change with the softness of the soil and the speed of the animal, and experts often disagreed over whether two prints came from one tiger or two. Critics argued that the counts tended to rise whenever officials were under pressure to show success.

Today the main tool is the camera trap: a weatherproof camera fixed to a tree, which takes a picture whenever an animal passes in front of it. Because the pattern of stripes on every tiger is unique, like a human fingerprint, a computer can match photographs and recognise individuals. Thousands of cameras are placed across a reserve for several weeks, and the results are analysed using a method known as capture-recapture.

The logic of capture-recapture is easiest to see with a simple example. Suppose cameras photograph forty different tigers in the first fortnight, and in the second fortnight they photograph forty again, of which twenty were already seen. Since half of the second sample had been 'captured' earlier, statisticians reason that the first sample probably represented about half the population, which is therefore around eighty. Real surveys use far more complex models, but the principle is the same.

Camera traps have drawbacks too. They are expensive, they can be stolen or damaged by elephants, and they work poorly for animals without distinctive markings. For such species, researchers increasingly turn to DNA extracted from droppings, which can identify individuals without the animal ever being seen.

What these methods share is a shift from guesswork to evidence that others can check. A count that can be repeated and verified, even if imperfect, is worth more than a confident figure that no one can test.

stimuli.title: The trouble with rent control
stimuli.content:
Few policies are as popular with voters, or as unpopular with economists, as rent control. When a city caps the rent that landlords may charge, tenants who already have homes are protected from sudden increases, and families who might otherwise be forced to move can stay near their schools and jobs. The appeal is easy to understand, especially in cities where rents have risen far faster than wages.

The difficulty lies in what happens next. If the permitted rent is well below what the market would bear, owning a flat to let becomes less rewarding. Some landlords sell their properties, others convert them into offices or holiday lets, and many simply leave flats empty rather than accept a low rent from a tenant they cannot easily remove. Builders, expecting controlled returns, put up fewer new rental homes. Over time, the supply of housing available for rent shrinks.

Those who already hold controlled tenancies benefit, often for decades. Newcomers to the city, who are frequently young and poor, find fewer homes on offer and may end up paying more in the uncontrolled part of the market or making informal payments to secure a flat. The policy thus divides tenants into insiders and outsiders, and the outsiders are not always better off than they would have been without it.

Maintenance suffers as well. A landlord who cannot raise the rent has little reason to repair a leaking roof, and tenants who fear losing a cheap flat are reluctant to complain. In some old city centres, buildings under long-standing rent control have decayed to the point of danger.

None of this means that tenants should be left at the mercy of the market. Many economists favour other remedies: allowing more homes to be built, offering housing allowances to poor families, or limiting how sharply rents may rise within an existing lease while letting them reset between tenants. Such measures are less eye-catching than a rent freeze, but they aim at the cause of high rents, a shortage of homes, rather than at its symptom.

stimuli.title: The month you were born
stimuli.content:
In many sports academies, a curious pattern appears when the players' birth dates are listed. Far more of them are born in the months just after the cut-off date used to group children by age than in the months just before it. The pattern has been found in football, cricket and ice hockey across several countries, and psychologists call it the relative age effect.

The explanation lies in the way children are sorted. If teams are formed by calendar year, a child born in January and one born in December of the same year play in the same age group, although the first is almost a year older. At the age of eight or nine, eleven months can make a large difference to height, strength and coordination. The older child is more likely to stand out in a trial, be picked for a better team and receive more coaching, which widens the gap still further. What began as an accident of the calendar is gradually mistaken for talent.

The effect does not stop at sport. Studies in several countries have found that, on average, the youngest children in a school class score slightly lower in early tests and are more often judged to have learning or behavioural difficulties. Much of this gap narrows as children grow older, but decisions taken early, such as placement in a slower stream, can have lasting consequences.

Curiously, the advantage is sometimes reversed at the highest level. A few studies suggest that among the relatively young players who do reach professional sport, a larger share go on to long careers, perhaps because they had to develop skill and resilience to compete with bigger rivals.

Remedies are simple in principle. Selectors can be shown each child's age in months and asked to judge performance against it; some academies have experimented with rotating the cut-off date each year, or with grouping children by physical development rather than birth date. None of these removes the effect entirely, but each reduces the chance that a selector confuses being older with being better.

stimuli.title: The many lives of bamboo
stimuli.content:
Bamboo is often called a tree, but it is in fact a giant grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on earth. Some species can grow (1) ______ a metre in a single day, and a new clump can be harvested within a few years, far sooner than most timber trees.

For centuries, rural communities in India's north-east have used bamboo for almost everything: houses, bridges, baskets, water pipes and even food, since its young shoots are cooked and eaten as a (2) ______. Because the plant regrows from its roots after cutting, a well-managed grove can supply material year after year without being (3) ______.

Bamboo's strength surprises many people. Weight for weight, some species are remarkably strong when pulled, which is why builders in parts of Asia still use bamboo poles for scaffolding on tall buildings. It is also light and (4) ______, so it bends in strong winds rather than snapping.

The plant does have limits. Untreated bamboo is easily attacked by insects and fungi, and it can rot within a few years if it is left in damp conditions. Simple treatments with salt solutions can extend its life many times over, but they are not yet widely (5) ______ by village craftsmen, many of whom have never been shown how to use them. Supporters argue that with better treatment and design, bamboo could replace some of the cement and steel used in rural housing, cutting both costs and the pollution that comes from making those materials.

stimuli.title: The real cost of free returns
stimuli.content:
Online shoppers have come to expect that anything they buy can be sent back free of charge. For retailers, generous return policies are a powerful way to (1) ______ customers who would otherwise hesitate to buy clothes or shoes they cannot try on. A buyer who knows she can return a dress is far more likely to order it, and perhaps to order two sizes at once.

The convenience, however, comes at a price that the shopper rarely sees. Every returned parcel must be collected, transported back to a warehouse, inspected and repackaged before it can be sold again. For low-priced goods, these steps can cost more than the item itself, so many returns are never put back on sale at all; they are sold off cheaply in bulk or simply (2) ______.

Returns also add to (3) ______. A parcel that travels to the customer and back again doubles the delivery journey, and the packaging used for it is often thrown away. Some estimates suggest that a significant share of everything bought online is returned, and the share is highest for (4) ______, where fit is hard to judge on a screen.

Retailers have begun to look for ways to reduce returns without losing customers. Better size charts, photographs taken from several angles and reviews that mention whether an item runs small or large all help buyers choose correctly the first time. A few companies have started to charge a small fee for returns, or to offer a discount to shoppers who (5) ______ to keep an item they are unsure about.

The broader lesson is that 'free' is seldom truly free. When a service costs the customer nothing, its cost is usually (6) ______ somewhere else, whether in higher prices, lower wages along the delivery chain, or a heavier burden on the environment.

stimuli.title: When rates rise, bonds fall
stimuli.content:
A government bond is a promise to pay its holder a fixed amount of interest every year and to return the original sum when the bond matures. Because the interest is fixed when the bond is issued, the bond's market price must **(1) adjust** whenever interest rates in the economy change.

Suppose a bond pays seven per cent a year, and soon afterwards new bonds are issued paying eight per cent. No investor will now pay full price for the old bond when a new one offers more, so the old bond's price must **(2) rise** until its fixed payments give a buyer roughly the same return as the new bonds. The opposite happens when rates fall: older bonds, paying more than new ones, become more **(3) attractive**, and their prices go up.

This is why bond prices and interest rates are said to be **(4) directly** related. The effect is strongest for bonds that have many years left to run, because their fixed payments stretch far into the future, so a change in rates affects a larger stream of income.

The relationship matters well beyond the bond market. Banks hold large amounts of government bonds, and a sharp rise in interest rates can reduce the value of these holdings and **(5) strengthen** their balance sheets. Investors and regulators therefore watch the expected path of interest rates closely, since even a small change can shift the value of portfolios worth billions. For an ordinary saver, the lesson is simpler: a bond held until it matures returns its full original sum, but one sold earlier may fetch less than was paid for it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
? ÷ 9 − 14 × 3 = 1,008 ÷ 24 + 5 × 7

solution.concept: Finish × and ÷ on both sides first, then undo the operations on ? in reverse order
solution.why_others_wrong: 315 subtracts 42 from 77 instead of adding it (35 × 9); 693 forgets the − 14 × 3 term (77 × 9); 1,197 divides 1,008 by 18 instead of 24 (56 + 35 + 42 = 133, × 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 640 + 18² = 7 × 68

solution.concept: Evaluate the known terms, isolate the percentage term, then convert: ?% of 640 = ? × 6.4
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 adds 324 instead of subtracting it (800 ÷ 6.4); 74.375 ignores the 18² term (476 ÷ 6.4); 2.375 divides by 64 instead of 6.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
2¾ + 3⅚ − 1⅝ = ?

solution.concept: Add and subtract the whole parts and the fractional parts separately, using the LCM 24 for the fractions
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 5/24 adds 1⅝ instead of subtracting it; 6 5/24 subtracts only the whole 1 and adds the ⅝; 3 23/24 subtracts 2 in the whole parts instead of 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.36 × 2.5 + 4.8 ÷ 0.12 − 1.9 = ?

solution.concept: Do × and ÷ before + and −; to divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by a power of 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 takes 4.8 ÷ 0.12 as 4 (dividing by 1.2); 399 takes it as 400 (dividing by 0.012); 42.8 adds the 1.9 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
√0.0169 + √1.69 + √169 = ?

solution.concept: The square root of a decimal has half as many decimal places: √0.0169 = 0.13, √1.69 = 1.3
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.6 takes √0.0169 as 1.3; 13.26 takes √1.69 as 0.13; 1.443 misplaces the decimal point in the sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√12 + √27 − √48)² = ?

solution.concept: Write each surd as a multiple of the same surd (here √3) before adding or subtracting
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 takes √48 as 3√3, leaving 2√3; 27 takes √48 as 2√3, leaving 3√3; 243 adds √48 instead of subtracting it (9√3, squared).

solution.concept: Recognise the identity a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²
solution.explanation: With a = 2.75 and b = 1.25 the expression is (a + b)² = (2.75 + 1.25)² = 4² = 16.
solution.shortcut: Spot the pattern a² + 2ab + b² instead of multiplying the decimals out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.125 adds only the two squares and drops the 2ab term; 4 forgets to square a + b; 2.25 uses (a − b)² = 1.5².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of (2¹⁰ − 2⁸) ÷ (2⁷ + 2⁶)?

solution.concept: Take the smallest power out as a common factor in the numerator and in the denominator
solution.explanation: Numerator: 2⁸(2² − 1) = 2⁸ × 3. Denominator: 2⁶(2 + 1) = 2⁶ × 3. So the value is 2⁸ ÷ 2⁶ = 2² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 divides 768 by 2⁷ alone; 12 divides it by 2⁶ alone; 2 subtracts the exponents inside each bracket (2¹⁰⁻⁸ ÷ 2⁷⁻⁶), which is not allowed for a sum or difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 4ˣ − 4ˣ⁻¹ = 24, what is the value of (2x)ˣ?

solution.concept: Take the smaller power out as a factor: 4ˣ − 4ˣ⁻¹ = 4ˣ⁻¹(4 − 1); then write both sides as powers of 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 rounds the solution to x = 3 (6³); 25 drops the half power and takes 5²; 3√3 solves 2x = 3 (forgetting the − 2), so x = 1.5 and 3^1.5 = 3√3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √0.444… + √2.777… + √0.111…, where each decimal has its last digit recurring.

solution.concept: Convert each recurring decimal to a fraction with denominator 9 (0.ddd… = d/9), then take square roots
solution.why_others_wrong: 3⅓ adds the fractions 4/9 + 25/9 + 1/9 and forgets the square roots; 2⅓ converts 2.777… as 1 + 7/9 = 16/9 (root 4/3); 8/9 takes the roots of the numerators but forgets that √9 = 3 in the denominator.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

solution.why_others_wrong: 21 adds 49 instead of subtracting it (338 ÷ 16 ≈ 21); 18 ignores the 35% term (289 ÷ 16 ≈ 18); 9 is 6 away from the exact value (about 15.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

(8.97 × 13.02 + 2.99 × 13.01) ÷ 5.98 ≈ ?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.4998 × ? + 1/0.0499 ≈ 61.97

solution.concept: 1/0.05 = 20; then undo the + and the × in reverse order
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 multiplies 42 by 0.5 instead of dividing; 164 adds 20 instead of subtracting it; 120 takes 1/0.05 as 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(? + 14.98% of 239.9) ÷ 6.02 ≈ 27.03 × 3.99 − √1023.6

solution.concept: Finish the right side, multiply back by 6, then remove the known part of the bracket
solution.why_others_wrong: 492 adds 36 instead of subtracting it; 456 is the value of the whole bracket, not of ?; 612 forgets the √1024 term (108 × 6 − 36).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?² + √4095.7 × 2.99 ≈ 24.02² + 3.98² (? is positive)

solution.concept: Round each term, isolate ?², then take the positive square root
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 keeps only the 24.02² term; 28 adds 192 instead of subtracting it (√784); 400 is ?², not ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
50, 61, 58, 69, 66, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 63 applies − 3 again instead of + 11; 74 adds the net change of a pair of steps (+ 8); 88 adds 11 twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
4, 7, 11, 18, ?, 47, 76

solution.concept: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 repeats the difference 7; 36 doubles 18; 22 adds the first difference 4 again. None of them gives 47 at the next step (18 + 25 = 43, 18 + 36 = 54, 18 + 22 = 40).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
81, 27, 54, 18, 36, 12, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 4 divides by 3 again; 36 repeats the previous high term; 6 halves 12 instead of doubling it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
100, 132, 148, 156, 160, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 32, 16, 8, 4, so the next difference is 2 and the term is 160 + 2 = 162.
solution.why_others_wrong: 164 adds 4 again; 161 halves twice and adds 1; 158 subtracts 2 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 4, 13, 38, 87, ?

solution.concept: The differences are the squares of odd numbers: 1², 3², 5², 7², …
solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 9, 25, 49 = 1², 3², 5², 7². The next is 9² = 81, so the term is 87 + 81 = 168.
solution.why_others_wrong: 151 adds 8², an even square; 136 adds 7² again; 187 adds 10², skipping 9².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
3, 15, 35, ?, 99, 143

solution.concept: Each term is the product of two consecutive odd numbers: 1 × 3, 3 × 5, 5 × 7, …
solution.explanation: 3 = 1 × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 35 = 5 × 7, so the missing term is 7 × 9 = 63; then 9 × 11 = 99 and 11 × 13 = 143. (Equivalently each term is one less than an even square: 4 − 1, 16 − 1, 36 − 1, 64 − 1, …)
solution.shortcut: Differences 12, 20, 28, 36, 44 rise by 8: 35 + 28 = 63.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 adds 20 again; 64 is 8² and forgets the − 1; 48 is 7² − 1, the pattern applied to an odd base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 3, 10, 15, 26, 35, ?

solution.concept: Odd positions are n² + 1 and even positions are n² − 1
solution.shortcut: Differences 1, 7, 5, 11, 9 alternate between two series rising by 4: the next difference is 15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 uses 7² − 1, the even-position rule; 49 forgets the ± 1 altogether; 44 adds 9 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
256, 320, 400, 500, 625, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 750 adds the last difference 125 again; 812.5 multiplies by 1.3; 1,250 doubles 625.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 32, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the product of the two terms before it
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 only doubles 32; 128 multiplies 32 by 4 instead of 8; 1,024 squares 32.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 6, 4, 8, 0, 16, ?

solution.concept: The differences are +1, −2, +4, −8, +16: they double in size and alternate in sign
solution.explanation: Differences: +1, −2, +4, −8, +16. The next difference is −32, so the term is 16 − 32 = −16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 adds 32 and ignores the alternating sign; 0 subtracts 16, repeating the size of the last step; −48 doubles the step twice (− 64).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 10, 26, 50, 122, ?

solution.concept: Each term is (a prime number)² + 1, taking the primes in order: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 145 uses 12, which is not prime; 290 uses 17 and skips 13; 226 uses 15, which is not prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 9, 25, 64, 169, ?

solution.concept: Take square roots: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 — each is the sum of the two before it
solution.explanation: √ of the terms: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Each is the sum of the previous two (2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13), so the next root is 8 + 13 = 21 and the term is 21² = 441.
steps: Rule: add the two previous roots
solution.why_others_wrong: 289 = 17² takes the roots as primes (2, 3, 5, … but 8 is not prime); 324 = 18² adds 5 to 13, repeating an earlier gap; 338 doubles 169.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 3, 10, 29, 74, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous term × 2 + a perfect square, the squares rising 1², 2², 3², …
solution.why_others_wrong: 164 adds 16 again; 148 only doubles; 223 uses × 3 + 1, which fits only the step 3 → 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 7, 23, 47, 119, 167, ?

solution.concept: Add 2 to each term: 4, 9, 25, 49, 121, 169 are the squares of consecutive primes
solution.explanation: Each term is p² − 2 for the primes p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. The next prime is 17, so the term is 17² − 2 = 287.
solution.why_others_wrong: 223 uses 15 and 254 uses 16, neither of which is prime; 359 uses 19 and skips 17.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 3, 8, ?, 3968

solution.why_others_wrong: 48 multiplies 8 by 6; 65 uses 8² + 1; 24 multiplies 8 by 3. None of them gives 3968 at the next step (48² − 1 = 2303, 65² − 1 = 4224, 24² − 1 = 575).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 9, 25, 48, 81, 121, 169

solution.concept: The terms are the squares of the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, …
solution.explanation: 1², 3², 5², 7², 9², 11², 13² = 1, 9, 25, 49, 81, 121, 169. The fourth term should be 49, not 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: 81, 121 and 25 are 9², 11² and 5² and fit the pattern.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 10, 7, 14, 12, 22, 19

solution.why_others_wrong: 7, 22 and 19 all fit; 22 looks wrong only if 12 is taken as correct (12 × 2 = 24).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 6, 3, 9, 4.5, 12.5, 6.75

solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5, 9 and 6.75 fit the rule; 6.75 confirms 13.5, since 12.5 ÷ 2 would be 6.25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 4, 6, 12, 36, 154, 876

solution.why_others_wrong: 36, 12 and 876 fit; 876 confirms 156, since 154 + 720 = 874.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 5, 14, 39, 89, 209, 378

solution.concept: The differences are the squares of consecutive primes: 2², 3², 5², 7², 11², 13²
solution.why_others_wrong: 39, 209 and 378 fit; the shown differences 50 and 120 both point to the single term 89, which should be 88.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve equations I and II and choose the relation between x and y that is true for every pair of their roots.
I. x² − 19x + 90 = 0
II. y² − 13y + 40 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each quadratic; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 9)(x − 10) = 0, so x = 9 or 10. II: (y − 5)(y − 8) = 0, so y = 5 or 8. The smallest x (9) is greater than the largest y (8), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from a sign slip that gives negative roots for I (−9 and −10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Work out the roots of both equations, then mark the relation between x and y.
I. x² + 5x − 84 = 0
II. y² − 16y + 63 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the two equations share a root, the relation can only be non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x + 12)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 7 or −12. II: (y − 7)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 7 or 9. x = 7 = y is possible, and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: Other pairs: x < y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common root 7; x ≥ y holds only for the pair x = y = 7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have only negative roots. Solve them and choose how x is related to y.
I. x² + 18x + 80 = 0
II. y² + 11y + 30 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: With all coefficients positive, both roots are negative; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x + 8)(x + 10) = 0, so x = −8 or −10. II: (y + 5)(y + 6) = 0, so y = −5 or −6. The largest x (−8) is below the smallest y (−6), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from comparing 8 and 10 with 5 and 6 without the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of I and II and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. 2x² − 11x + 12 = 0
II. y² − 7y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: If the roots of one equation lie on both sides of a root of the other, no relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (2x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 1.5 or 4. II: (y − 2)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 2 or 5. x = 4 is above y = 2 but below y = 5, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only the pair x = 4, y = 2; x ≤ y and x < y use x = 1.5 or the pair x = 4, y = 5.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear with decimal coefficients and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 0.4x + 1.2 = 0.25x + 2.1
II. y² − 13y + 42 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Collect the x-terms in the linear equation; a value shared with the quadratic makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 0.4x − 0.25x = 2.1 − 1.2, so 0.15x = 0.9 and x = 6. II: (y − 6)(y − 7) = 0, so y = 6 or 7. x = y when y = 6 and x < y when y = 7, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses y = 6; x > y comes from moving 1.2 to the right side with the wrong sign (0.15x = 3.3 ⇒ x = 22).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations, whose roots are fractions, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 6x² − 19x + 15 = 0
II. 10y² − 29y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term using factors of a × c; check for a common root
solution.explanation: I: 6x² − 9x − 10x + 15 = (2x − 3)(3x − 5) = 0, so x = 1.5 or 5/3. II: 10y² − 15y − 14y + 21 = (2y − 3)(5y − 7) = 0, so y = 1.5 or 1.4. x = y = 1.5 is possible and every other pair has x > y, so x ≥ y.
steps: Other pairs: x > y ⇒ x ≥ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the common root 1.5; x < y comes from taking 5y − 7 = 0 as y = 7/2 = 3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is a perfect square. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 4x² + 12x + 9 = 0
II. y² + 3y + 2 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root; see where it falls among the other equation's roots
solution.explanation: I: (2x + 3)² = 0, so x = −1.5 only. II: (y + 1)(y + 2) = 0, so y = −1 or −2. −1.5 lies between −2 and −1: it is greater than −2 but less than −1. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y compares −1.5 with −2 only; x ≤ y and x < y compare it with −1 only.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is an exponential equation. Find every real value of x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. 2^(x²) = 16ˣ
II. y² − 9y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Write both sides with base 2 and equate the exponents; do not divide by x, which could be zero
solution.explanation: I: 16ˣ = 2^(4x), so x² = 4x, i.e. x(x − 4) = 0 and x = 0 or 4. II: (y − 4)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 5. x = 4 = y is possible and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: x = y = 4 possible; else x < y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common value 4; x ≥ y holds only for x = y = 4, and dividing by x (losing x = 0) still leaves x = 4 < 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains fractions in x (x ≠ 0, −1). Clear them, solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 3/x + 4/(x + 1) = 2
II. 4y² − 8y + 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Multiply through by x(x + 1) to get a quadratic; check that the roots do not make a denominator zero
solution.explanation: I: 3(x + 1) + 4x = 2x(x + 1), so 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0 = (2x + 1)(x − 3), giving x = 3 or −0.5. II: (2y − 1)(2y − 3) = 0, so y = 0.5 or 1.5. x = 3 is above both y values, but x = −0.5 is below both. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only x = 3; x ≤ y and x < y use only x = −0.5.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The coefficients below are large. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 46x + 528 = 0
II. y² − 47y + 552 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find two numbers with the given sum and product; near-equal roots must be compared pair by pair
solution.explanation: I: 22 + 24 = 46 and 22 × 24 = 528, so x = 22 or 24. II: 23 + 24 = 47 and 23 × 24 = 552, so y = 23 or 24. x = 22 is below both y values, but x = 24 is above y = 23. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.shortcut: Half the sum gives the middle: 46/2 = 23 ⇒ roots 23 ± 1; 47/2 = 23.5 ⇒ roots 23.5 ± 0.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≥ y and x > y use only x = 24; x < y uses only x = 22 and misses the pair x = 24, y = 23.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1234⁵⁶⁷ + 5678¹²³?

solution.concept: Only the unit digits matter: powers of 4 end in 4, 6, 4, 6, … and powers of 8 cycle 8, 4, 2, 6
solution.explanation: 1234⁵⁶⁷ ends like 4⁵⁶⁷; an odd power of 4 ends in 4. 5678¹²³ ends like 8¹²³; 123 = 4 × 30 + 3, so it ends like 8³ = 512, i.e. in 2. The sum ends in 4 + 2 = 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 multiplies the unit digits (4 × 2) instead of adding them; 0 takes 4⁵⁶⁷ as ending in 6 (an even power); 2 is the unit digit of the second term alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The HCF of two numbers is 27 and their LCM is 2,079. If one of the numbers lies between 250 and 300, what is the other number?

solution.concept: Write the numbers as 27a and 27b with a, b co-prime; then 27ab = LCM
solution.explanation: 2,079 ÷ 27 = 77 = 7 × 11, so (a, b) = (1, 77) or (7, 11). The pairs are 27 and 2,079, or 189 and 297. Only the second pair has a number between 250 and 300 (297), so the other number is 189.
solution.why_others_wrong: 297 is the number in the given range, not the other one; 77 is LCM ÷ HCF; 231 divides 2,079 by 9 instead of using the HCF 27.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many even factors does 720 have?

solution.concept: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5; an even factor must contain at least one 2
solution.explanation: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. All factors: (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 30. Odd factors use 2⁰ only: (2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 6. Even factors = 30 − 6 = 24 (equivalently, choose 2¹ to 2⁴: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24).
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 counts all the factors; 6 counts only the odd factors; 20 uses 2⁴ × 3 × 5 and misses the 3².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest positive number that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5, a remainder of 3 when divided by 7 and a remainder of 4 when divided by 9?

solution.concept: Satisfy the conditions one at a time: list numbers fitting two of them (they repeat every LCM), then test the third
solution.explanation: Numbers leaving 4 on division by 9: 4, 13, 22, 31, … The first that also leaves 3 on division by 7 is 31; such numbers repeat every 63: 31, 94, 157, … Testing division by 5: 31 → 1, 94 → 4, 157 → 2 ✓. So the number is 157.
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 and 94 satisfy the conditions for 7 and 9 but not for 5; 472 also works but is the next such number (157 + 315), not the smallest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A's salary is 25% more than B's, and B's salary is 20% less than C's. A's salary is what percentage of C's?

solution.concept: Chain the multipliers: A = 1.25 B and B = 0.80 C
solution.explanation: B = 0.8 C, so A = 1.25 × 0.8 C = C. A's salary is 100% of C's.
solution.shortcut: +25% undoes −20% exactly, because 1.25 = 1 ÷ 0.8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 105% adds the two percentages (+25 − 20 = +5); 95% subtracts them the other way; 125% compares A with B instead of with C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is increased by 30% and the result is then decreased by 30%. The final value is 819. What was the original number?

solution.explanation: The net multiplier is 1.3 × 0.7 = 0.91, so the original number = 819 ÷ 0.91 = 900.
solution.why_others_wrong: 819 assumes +30% and −30% cancel; 1,170 undoes only the 30% fall (819 ÷ 0.7); 745.29 applies the two changes to 819 again instead of reversing them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a class, 40% of the students are girls. 25% of the boys and 35% of the girls scored a distinction. What percentage of the whole class scored a distinction?

solution.concept: The overall rate is a weighted average of the two rates, weighted by the share of boys and girls
solution.explanation: Take 100 students: 60 boys and 40 girls. Distinctions: 25% of 60 = 15 and 35% of 40 = 14, so 29 out of 100 = 29%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% is the simple average of 25% and 35%; 31% swaps the weights (40% boys, 60% girls); 60% adds the two rates.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The radius of a cylinder is increased by 20% and its height is decreased by 20%. What is the percentage change in its volume?

solution.concept: Volume ∝ r²h, so the radius change enters twice: multiply 1.2 × 1.2 × 0.8
solution.explanation: New volume ÷ old volume = 1.2² × 0.8 = 1.44 × 0.8 = 1.152. The volume rises by 15.2%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No change' assumes +20% and −20% cancel; '4% decrease' treats volume as r × h (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96); '44% increase' squares the radius change but forgets the height.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a test, a candidate who scored 30% of the maximum marks failed by 15 marks, while another who scored 40% got 35 marks more than the pass mark. What percentage of the maximum marks is needed to pass?

solution.concept: Both statements describe the same pass mark: set 30% of M + 15 equal to 40% of M − 35
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% takes the mid-point of 30% and 40%; 37% subtracts 15 from the 40% score (200 − 15 = 185) instead of 35; 30% is the failing candidate's own score.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car loses 15% of its value every year (on its value at the start of that year). After how many complete years will its value first fall below half of the purchase price?

solution.concept: Depreciation compounds: value after n years = P × 0.85ⁿ; find the first n with 0.85ⁿ < 0.5
solution.explanation: 0.85² = 0.7225, 0.85³ ≈ 0.614, 0.85⁴ ≈ 0.522 (still above half) and 0.85⁵ ≈ 0.444 (below half). So it first falls below half after 5 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years stops too early (52.2% of the price is left); 3 years uses straight-line loss (50 ÷ 15 ≈ 3.3, rounded down); 6 years is one year after it has already fallen below half.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family spends 40% of its income on food, 15% on rent and 25% on other items, and saves the rest. Its income rises by 10%, food costs rise by 25%, rent rises by 20% and other spending does not change. By what percentage do its savings change?

solution.concept: Take income = 100; update each spending head separately and recompute savings
solution.explanation: Old: spending 40 + 15 + 25 = 80, savings 20. New: income 110; food 50, rent 18, others 25, total 93; savings 17. Savings fall from 20 to 17, i.e. by 15%.
solution.why_others_wrong: '10% increase' assumes savings move with income; '3% decrease' gives the fall in rupees per 100 of old income, not as a percentage of the old savings; '15% increase' gets the sign of the change wrong.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Town P has 75,000 people and its population grows by 4% a year. Town Q has 90,000 people and its population falls by 5% a year. Both rates are applied on the population at the start of each year. After 2 years, which town has more people, and by how many?

solution.concept: Apply each rate twice (compounding) and compare
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Same population' applies the rates as simple (non-compounding) changes: 75,000 × 1.08 = 90,000 × 0.90 = 81,000; 'Town P, by 105' reverses the difference; 'Town Q, by 225' compounds Q's fall but treats P's growth as simple (81,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the fourth proportional to 12, 18 and 30?

solution.concept: x is the fourth proportional to a, b, c when a : b = c : x, so x = bc ÷ a
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 sets up 18 : 12 = 30 : x (the ratio reversed); 36 adds the difference 18 − 12 to 30 instead of keeping the ratio; 540 forgets to divide by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A purse contains 50-paise, ₹1 and ₹2 coins worth ₹185 in all. There are twice as many ₹1 coins as 50-paise coins, and 5 fewer ₹2 coins than ₹1 coins. How many ₹2 coins are there?

solution.concept: Let the number of 50-paise coins be n and write the total value in rupees
solution.explanation: 50-paise coins: n; ₹1 coins: 2n; ₹2 coins: 2n − 5. Value: 0.5n + 2n + 2(2n − 5) = 6.5n − 10 = 185, so n = 30. ₹2 coins = 2 × 30 − 5 = 55.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 is the number of 50-paise coins; 60 is the number of ₹1 coins; 50 subtracts 10 instead of 5 from 60.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (a + b) : (b + c) : (c + a) = 6 : 7 : 8 and a + b + c = 14, what is the value of c?

solution.concept: Adding the three sums gives 2(a + b + c); this fixes the scale k of the ratio
steps: Sum of the three = 2(a + b + c) = 28
solution.why_others_wrong: 14/3 is the value of a and 10/3 the value of b; 8 is a + b, not c.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money is divided among P, Q and R. P gets ₹300 more than two-fifths of the sum, Q gets ₹500 less than one-third of the sum, and R gets ₹2,600. What is the total sum?

solution.concept: Write each share in terms of the total S and use P + Q + R = S
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,900 is P's share; ₹9,750 forgets the ₹300 and ₹500 adjustments (4S/15 = 2,600); ₹10,500 moves the adjustments across with the wrong signs (4S/15 = 2,800).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average present age of a husband, his wife and their child is 27 years. Three years ago, the average age of the wife and the child was 20 years. What is the husband's present age?

solution.concept: Convert averages to totals, and move the past total to the present by adding 3 years for each person
solution.explanation: Present total of all three = 3 × 27 = 81. Three years ago, wife + child = 2 × 20 = 40, so now they total 40 + 6 = 46. Husband = 81 − 46 = 35 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 forgets to add 3 years to each of the wife and child; 38 adds 3 years only once; 47 subtracts 6 years instead of adding them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A father is as many years old as his son is months old. The sum of their ages is 65 years. How old is the father?

solution.concept: The son's age in months is 12 times his age in years, so the father is 12 times as old as the son
solution.explanation: If the son is s years old, he is 12s months old, so the father is 12s years old. 12s + s = 65 gives s = 5, and the father is 60.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 years is the son's age; 55 takes the son as 10; 52 splits 65 in the ratio 4 : 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When Ravi was born, his father was 28 years old. Now the father is 1.8 times as old as Ravi. After how many years will the father be 1.5 times as old as Ravi?

solution.concept: The age gap (28 years) never changes; use it to find the present ages, then set up the future ratio
solution.explanation: Father − Ravi = 28 and Father = 1.8 × Ravi, so 0.8 × Ravi = 28: Ravi is 35 and the father 63. Then 63 + n = 1.5(35 + n) gives 0.5n = 10.5 and n = 21.
solution.shortcut: When F = 1.5R, the gap 28 = 0.5R, so R = 56: that is 56 − 35 = 21 years from now.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.5 forgets to divide by 0.5; 28 is the age gap; 35 is Ravi's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family has a father, a mother and two children. The four ages now add up to 104 years. The father is 5 years older than the mother, and the elder child is 3 years older than the younger. When the younger child was born, the ages of the other three members added up to 64 years. What is the mother's present age?

solution.concept: Going back y years (the younger child's age) takes y years off each of the other three members
solution.explanation: Let the younger child be y. Then the other three now total 104 − y, and y years ago they totalled 104 − y − 3y = 104 − 4y = 64, so y = 10. The elder child is 13, so the parents total 104 − 23 = 81. With the father 5 years older, the mother is (81 − 5) ÷ 2 = 38.
solution.why_others_wrong: 43 is the father's age; 40.5 splits 81 equally and ignores the 5-year gap; 28 is the mother's age when the younger child was born.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of A, B and C is 60 kg. The average weight of A and B is 56 kg, and that of B and C is 61 kg. What is B's weight?

solution.concept: Convert each average to a total; B is counted in both pair totals
solution.explanation: A + B + C = 180, A + B = 112 and B + C = 122. Adding the pair totals counts B twice: 112 + 122 = 234 = 180 + B, so B = 54 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 58 kg is A's weight; 68 kg is C's weight; 56 kg is the average of A and B, not B's own weight.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop sold 120 items at an average price of ₹45 on Monday and 80 items at an average price of ₹60 on Tuesday. What was the average price of all the items sold on the two days?

solution.concept: Average of all items = total takings ÷ total items
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52.50 is the simple average of 45 and 60, which ignores the numbers sold; ₹54 swaps the weights; ₹10,200 is the total takings, not the average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average monthly salary of 15 workers is ₹18,000. A worker earning ₹24,000 leaves, and two new workers with equal salaries join. The average salary of the group is now ₹17,500. What is the salary of each new worker?

solution.concept: Track the total: remove the leaving worker's salary, then compare with the new total for the new group size
solution.explanation: Old total = 15 × 18,000 = ₹2,70,000. After the worker leaves: ₹2,46,000 for 14 workers. With two more there are 17 workers and the total is 17 × 17,500 = ₹2,97,500. The two new salaries add up to 2,97,500 − 2,46,000 = ₹51,500, so each is ₹25,750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹51,500 is the two new salaries together; ₹17,000 counts the new group as 16 workers; ₹13,750 forgets to remove the leaving worker's ₹24,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of seven consecutive multiples of 3 is 45. What is the product of the smallest and the largest of them?

solution.concept: Consecutive multiples of 3 are equally spaced, so their average is the middle (4th) term
solution.explanation: The middle term is 45, so the numbers are 36, 39, 42, 45, 48, 51 and 54. The product of the smallest and largest is 36 × 54 = 1,944.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,025 = 45², the middle term squared; 1,989 = 39 × 51, the second and sixth terms; 2,016 = 42 × 48, the third and fifth terms.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a class, the 30 boys have an average height of 150 cm and the girls an average height of 140 cm; the average height of the whole class is 146 cm. Five boys with an average height of 152 cm leave the class, and five new girls with an average height of 138 cm join it. What is the new average height of the class?

solution.concept: First find the number of girls from the weighted average, then update the total height
solution.explanation: 30 × 150 + 140g = 146(30 + g) gives 4,500 + 140g = 4,380 + 146g, so g = 20 and the class has 50 students. Total height = 7,300 cm. Remove 5 × 152 = 760 and add 5 × 138 = 690: new total 7,230 cm for 50 students, so the new average is 144.6 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 145 cm assumes the leaving boys and joining girls are at their groups' averages (150 and 140); 146 cm assumes the average does not change because the class size is the same; 147.4 cm swaps the 760 and the 690.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader buys 25 kg of tea for ₹6,000 and sells all of it at ₹270 per kg. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Profit % = (SP − CP) ÷ CP × 100, with both prices for the same quantity
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.11% divides the profit by the selling price (30 ÷ 270); 30% takes the ₹30 profit per kg as a percentage; 112.5% is SP as a percentage of CP.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper sells rice at its cost price but uses a false weight of 960 g in place of 1 kg. What is his gain percentage?

solution.explanation: For every 960 g he gives, he charges the cost of 1,000 g. Gain = 40 g on 960 g = 40 ÷ 960 × 100 = 4⅙%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4% divides the 40 g by 1,000 g instead of by the 960 g actually given; 40% misplaces the decimal; 3.85% divides by 1,040 g.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells an article to B at a profit of 10%, B sells it to C at a profit of 15%, and C sells it to D at a loss of 10%. If D pays ₹22,770, at what price did A buy it?

solution.concept: Successive selling prices multiply the cost by 1.10, 1.15 and 0.90
